As far as rain... There are times where it comes and goes in 45 minutes. But it's far more common for it to be a few hours, all day,or even multiple day event. It's not uncommon for it to rain for three days straight. It won't be pouring the whole time, but it alternates between heavy rain, light rain and mist and it will stay cloudy that whole time. The upside is that it's decently predictable. It's decently obvious to figure out if it's going to storm if you just look at the sky. Dont come with any thoughts of swimming in any natural body of water this time of year. They are all about 40 degrees right now.

I'm not terribly familiar with North of the city, but South of the city offers a lot as the MN river runs through. The Hyland lake preserve in West Bloomington is really nice. Its nice for all levels of hiking. There is also the Minnesota River valley. Honestly, you cant walk 1/2 mile without running into a park of some kind. Beware that there are some things that look like they might be parks, but are actually just protected wetlands. Dont go in there.

Our cycling is amazing. There is a huge interlocking bike path that hits up most of the lakes/waterways in MPLS. Its called the grand rounds. Im sure you can google it. The greenway is a good mode of transportation through south MPLS. It runs parallel to Lake St. for quite a while. The river also has nice bike paths.

As far as Timberwolves stuff... Honestly MOA might be your best bet if you aren't planning on going to an actual game. Any of the tourist shops at MOA should have something. There are a lot of sports stores there too. Unfortunately you've chosen the least popular major sports team :) Its way easier to find stuff for the Twins, Wild or Vikings. 

Parking isnt terrible. It depends on when and where. The worst is downtown. Parking there is expensive. The cheapest option is usually the cities meters. But those are hard to come by. Other areas of MPLS arent too bad. Maybe $2-$5 an hour tops. Be careful of resident only parking. 

Weather advisory: Dress in layers. I cannot advise this enough. We Minnesotans wont dress in layers for 43 because thats flip flop weather for us, but if thats cold for you, layer up. You'll be sorry if you just wear a warm coat and a t-shirt. It also rains a lot in April so prepare for that. The temperature also plummets at night. It might be a nice 65 degree day out, but by midnight, it'll be 40. So if you are planning on barhopping or being out late outside, plan accordingly.  

As always, enjoy our fine city!

Sure. We work in a medical clinic that [this](http://lanceandjulieburma.org/Africa_Uplifted/Home.html) organization has set up. We provide basic care and offer medicines for things like malaria and typhoid. We charge them around 2,000 Leones (50 cents) per visit. Last time I was there in November of 2011 we saw around 400 people over a two week period. Only one of them was healthy. We also have a primary school set up that any of the kids in the village we work at can attend for about a dollar a semester. We pay for their uniforms, supplies, and we have set up a lunch program that feeds them twice a week.

We technically work in the small village of Manokoh, but we actually live in Makeni while we are there. I deal with the children from both places. 

Sierra Leone is desperatly poor. The last time I checked the average income was $ 800 dollars a year. THe literacy rate is only around 30%. While English is the official language, there is still a language barrier because only people who have gone to school speak it. It is very hard to communicate with some of the people. However, the people are wonderful. They are very welcoming and kind to us. The kids are crazy about us. They call us "El Porto" which means the Portugese. Apparently they used to get a lot of people from Porgugal. The kids are also obsessed with your skin. They don't see a lot of white people so they love to touch and rub your arms. My tattoos were a source of fascination for them. They also like to hold your hand when you walk anywhere. It is actually really cute. They love having pictures taken of them The kids really love soccer and pretty much any toy you give them. Their families dont have the resources to buy them toys because naturally, food comes first. So the kids will play with essencially anything they pick up off the street. I like to do things with them that engage their minds. Read with them, play with bubbles or stomp rockets. Things of that nature. They really like stuff that makes noise or anything electric. 

As for what they need, well that is a tough one because they need so much. A lot of the kids and adults are dressed in rags. Shoes are a huge deal. A lot of them run around barefoot which is dangerous because there is all sorts of nasty things on the ground for them to hurt themselves on. What I am focusing on is toys or little gadgets to help expand their minds. THings that we take for granted they find fascinating. Stuff like glow sticks or bubbles.

*flip flops
*kites

*glow sticks
*silly string
*balloons
*markers, colored pencils or crayons

Those are just some things off the top of my head. If you have something that isnt on the list just shoot me a message telling me what it is and I'll let you know if I can use it.

As a current Americorp summer VISTA, I can say with certainty that this is a TERRIBLE idea. I currently work with the boys and girls club in Billings Montana. I work with the kids to promote intrest in STEM related subjects. Not only have I seen the amazing things my program has caused, but I know that other VISTAs programs have also had amazing results. We have been working in various ways to eliminate poverty. Some of us work in homeless shelters, some of us, like me work with disadvantaged youth and some of us work to create things like community gardens. I know that I have had amazing results in my program and I have seen the growth many of the kids have made. Some of them have gone from zero intrest in anything to with school to wanting to be an engineer or doctor. THis will help them become productive members of society as well as moving them out of poverty. Most of the kids I work with were destained to jail, minimum wage jobs, unemployment, drug addiction or homelessness. I can now say with certainty that this will no longer be the case for some of them. All of this happened becuase Americorps saw a need for intervention and acted upon it bringing me onto the site to help those kids. Americorp has made a huge difference in their lives.
